propositions.text: The principal and associate Appellants, both Nepalese nationals, appeal the RPD decision denying refugee protection.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX (the "principal Appellant") and XXXX XXXX XXXX (the "associate Appellant"), who are both nationals of Nepal, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying their claim for refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that the Nepalese principal and associate Appellants appeal the RPD's denial of refugee protection.

propositions.text: Appellants submit new evidence under IRPA 110(4) and request an oral hearing under IRPA 110(6).
propositions.quote: The Appellants have submitted new evidence with the appeal as referred to in subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1 and request an oral hearing be held pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Appellants ask RAD to set aside RPD decision and find them Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The Appellants ask that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute a decision with its own determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

propositions.text: Alternatively, Appellants request RAD refer matter back to RPD with a differently constituted panel.
propositions.quote: In the alternative, the Appellants request that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD with a differently constituted panel.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants submit new evidence, request an oral hearing, ask RAD to set aside the RPD decision or alternatively refer back to RPD with a new panel.

propositions.text: RAD confirms RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under IRPA 111(1)(a).
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision and dismisses the appeal under IRPA 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: Appellants alleged threats and extortion by Biplav Maoist faction in Nepal in their Basis of Claim forms.
propositions.quote: The Appellants alleged before the RPD that they are being threatened and extorted in Nepal by members of the Biplav Maoist faction in their local area. Their allegations of harm are set out in their Basis of Claim (BOC) forms.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellants alleged threats and extortion by Biplav Maoists in Nepal in their Basis of Claim forms before the RPD.

propositions.text: RPD hearing held Nov 2, 2017; RPD rejected claim finding an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The Appellants' hearing for refugee protection was held on November 2, 2017. In an oral decision on the same day, the RPD rejected the Appellants' claim finding that the Appellants had an Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Appellants argue RPD erred in assessing IFA and documentary evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its assessment of the IFA and in its treatment of the documentary evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD rejected the claim on Nov 2, 2017, finding an IFA in Kathmandu; Appellants argue RPD erred on IFA and evidence.

propositions.text: RAD reviews RPD decisions on correctness standard for law and fact findings without oral credibility issues.
propositions.quote: As held by the Federal Court of Appeal in Huruglica,3 the RAD must review RPD decisions on a correctness standard with respect to questions of law and findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) which raise no issue of the credibility of oral evidence.

propositions.text: More deference may be required when RPD assesses oral evidence advantageously.
propositions.quote: More deference may be required when the RPD is in an advantageous position with respect to the assessment of oral evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD reviews RPD decisions on correctness standard for law and fact, with more deference for oral evidence credibility assessments.

propositions.text: Appellants submitted 24 news articles and National Human Rights Commission press releases as new evidence.
propositions.quote: In support of this appeal, the Appellants submitted approximately 24 news media articles,4 as well as a series of "press releases" from the National Human Rights Commission in Nepal as proposed new evidence in this appeal.

propositions.text: Appellants say articles contradict IRB's assertion that IFA is viable in Kathmandu and prove agents of persecution will find them there.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellants submit that the articles clearly contradict the assertion of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) that a viable IFA is available in Kathmandu. The Appellants submit that this evidence proves that the agents of persecution will find them in Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants submitted news articles and press releases as new evidence, arguing they contradict IRB's IFA finding and show persecution risk in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Under IRPA 110(4), new evidence must arise after claim rejection or be previously unavailable or unpresentable.
propositions.quote: Subsection 110(4) of the IRPA provides that the Appellants may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that they could not reasonably have been expected6 in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.

propositions.text: Appellants must make full submissions explaining how new evidence meets IRPA 110(4) and relates to them.
propositions.quote: It is for the Appellants to make full and detailed submissions in their Memorandum about how any proposed new evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) and how that evidence relates to the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: The court states IRPA 110(4) limits new evidence to post-rejection or unavailable evidence; Appellants must fully explain its relevance.

propositions.text: Three articles on bomb blasts, eleven on authorities' active stance, and four on FCAN shooting arose after claim rejection and meet IRPA 110(4).
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the three articles relating to "bomb blasts;"8 the eleven articles describing9 that the authorities have taken an active stance in protecting the public from potential violent activities associated with the efforts of the breakaway Chand CPN Maoists (Biplav); and a series of four articles10 linked to the shooting of the President of Federation of Contractors Association of Nepal (FCAN), all arose following the rejection of the Appellants' claim, hence, they meet the basic requirements of subsection 110(4).

propositions.text: These articles are credible, relevant, new, and admitted as new evidence in this appeal.
propositions.quote: In respect to assessing the adapted Raza factors endorsed in Singh,11 the RAD notes the articles are credible, relevant and new. The RAD finds the articles will be admitted as new evidence in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds certain articles credible, relevant, new, and admits them as new evidence meeting IRPA 110(4).

propositions.text: RAD may hold hearing if documentary evidence raises serious credibility issue central to refugee claim and could justify claim outcome.
propositions.quote: The RAD may hold a hearing if, in its opinion, there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3) of the IRPA that raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD may hold a hearing if documentary evidence raises serious credibility issues central to the refugee claim.

propositions.text: Appellants provide little explanation how articles relate to Biplav Maoists locating them in IFA location.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that the Appellants provide very little explanation as to how any of the articles submitted relate to the ability of the local Biplav Maoists from their home area to locate them in the IFA location.

propositions.text: Articles confirm Biplav Maoists involved in anti-election violence focused on Nepali Congress Party, not National Democratic Party.
propositions.quote: The RAD's review of the articles relating to the December 2017 bomb blasts in the Kathmandu area confirm that the Biplav Maoists are involved in anti-election related violence, which appears to be focused towards the Nepali Congress Party. The RAD notes the principal Appellant has stated that he was a member of the Rastriya Prajatantra Party Nepal (National Democratic Party) in his local area.

propositions.text: Articles do not show attacks linked to extortion or pursuit of individuals.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that none of the articles address any interaction with the National Democratic Party, nor do they provide any indication that the individuals associated with the so-called attacks were involved in extortion activities or the pursuit of other individuals.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants gave little explanation how articles relate to Biplav Maoists locating them; articles show anti-election violence not linked to extortion or their party.

propositions.text: Two articles describe authorities actively arresting individuals involved and preventing future disruption.
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds it of interest that two of the three articles13 describe that the authorities have taken an active interest in the arrest of the individuals involved and the prevention of future disruption through the pursuit and arrest of any individuals who are associated with the potential violence.

propositions.text: Articles confirm active and functioning state protection mechanism is in place.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the articles confirm that an active and fully functioning state protection mechanism is in place.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds articles show authorities actively arresting perpetrators and confirm a functioning state protection mechanism.

propositions.text: Seven articles confirm authorities actively protect public from violent activities of breakaway Chand CPN Maoists (Biplav).
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that seven additional articles14 confirm that the authorities have taken an active stance in protecting the public from potential violent activities associated with the efforts of the breakaway Chand CPN Maoists (Biplav) and their associates.

propositions.text: One article states law enforcement deployed special teams to arrest senior CPN leaders to curb violence.
propositions.quote: One article states, "the law enforcement agency has already deployed special teams to identify and arrest senior leaders of the CPN, which is the only force that is objecting to the elections ... If central leaders are arrested, it would be easier to curb the violent activities launched by the Chand-led CPN."

propositions.text: This confirms government intent and actions to provide state protection to all citizens.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds this further confirms the intent and actions of the government in providing state protection to all of its citizens.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds articles confirm authorities actively protect public from Biplav Maoists and government intent to provide state protection.

propositions.text: Four articles linked to FCAN president shooting show authorities investigated intensively and arrested five gang members.
propositions.quote: One of the articles titled, "Shooter among five arrested; extortion was the motive," confirms that the authorities conducted an intensive investigation, as well as generally increased the security activities in the Kathmandu valley, which led to the arrest of five gang members associated with the crime.

propositions.text: Shooting appears to be gang crime unrelated to CPN Maoists; authorities reacted swiftly, showing effective state protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that this appears to be a crime perpetrated by a gang of criminals with no linkage to the CPN Maoists. The RAD finds that as much as an individual was shot by criminals, the authorities reacted swiftly and apprehended the criminals, again demonstrating that state protection was effective.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds FCAN shooting was gang crime unrelated to Maoists; authorities reacted swiftly, showing effective state protection.

propositions.text: Articles show Biplav Maoists exist in Kathmandu involved in terrorist activities disrupting elections.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the articles submitted as new evidence indicate that Biplav Maoists do exist in Kathmandu and that they are primarily involved in terrorist type activities focused on disrupting the current election.

propositions.text: Articles do not show linkage between Kathmandu Biplav Maoists and home area group, extortion activities, or communication ability.
propositions.quote: The articles do not provide persuasive evidence that: * these individuals have any linkage to the Biplav Maoist group in their home area; * that they are involved in extortion related activities; and, * that the local Biplav group in their home area have any ability to communicate with other related groups.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds articles show Kathmandu Biplav Maoists involved in terrorism but no linkage to home area group or extortion activities.

propositions.text: Appellants' own evidence confirms active and functioning state protection in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: As much as the Appellants have alleged that Kathmandu is not a safe location in which to reside, the Appellants own evidence confirms that there is an active and functioning state protection mechanism in place to protect them should they encounter problems.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants' evidence confirms active and functioning state protection in Kathmandu despite their safety allegations.

propositions.text: Remaining articles arose before claim rejection and do not meet IRPA 110(4) requirements.
propositions.quote: The remaining articles16 do not meet the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA in that they arose prior to the rejection of the Appellants' claim before the RPD.

propositions.text: Appellants did not explain why these older documents should be admitted as new evidence.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not provided any addition submissions as to why these documents should be admitted as new evidence.

propositions.text: RAD will not admit these older articles as new evidence in this appeal.
propositions.quote: The RAD will not admit these articles as new evidence in this appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds remaining articles arose before claim rejection, Appellants gave no explanation, and refuses to admit them as new evidence.

propositions.text: Most National Human Rights Commission press releases arose after claim rejection, meeting IRPA 110(4).
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed the "press releases" from the National Human Rights Commission, Nepal.17 The RAD notes the majority of the documents arose following the rejection of the Appellants' claim for refugee protection, meeting the basic requirement of subsection 110(4).

propositions.text: Appellants did not explain how press releases relate to or support their allegations.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have not provided any explanation as to how these "press releases" relate to or support their allegations.

propositions.text: RAD Rules require appellants to file record including RPD decision, hearing transcript, refused documents, and detailed submissions on errors and evidence relevance.
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that Rule 3(3)(g) of the RAD Rules requires that the Appellants before the RAD must file a record that includes, inter alia, the RPD's decision; all or part of the transcript of the RPD hearing; any documents the RPD refused to accept, but that the Appellants want to rely on in the appeal; as well as the Appellants' Memorandum containing full and detailed submissions regarding: (i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal, (ii) where the errors are located in the written reasons for the Refugee Protection Division's decision that the appellant is appealing or in the transcript or in any audio or other electronic recording of the Refugee Protection Division hearing, (iii) how any documentary evidence referred to in paragraph (e) meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Act and how that evidence relates to the appellant.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds most press releases arose after claim rejection but Appellants gave no explanation; RAD rules require detailed submissions and record filing.

propositions.text: Appellants' submissions on new evidence are vague or absent, especially regarding press releases.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the Appellants' submissions accompanying the new evidence are generally vague, and that the submissions in respect of the press releases are absent.

propositions.text: Federal Court states appellants must explain how documents could affect application merits.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court has stated that Appellants have the obligation to explain how the documents submitted could have affected the merits of the application.

propositions.text: It is insufficient to submit information hoping decision-maker will find reason to agree; appellants must demonstrate RPD errors with evidence or law.
propositions.quote: It is insufficient to submit to a decision-maker [translation] "information in a bundle hoping that they would find a reason to agree" with an applicant.21 Rather, the Appellants have the burden of demonstrating how the RPD erred in drawing that finding with reference to the evidence, jurisprudence or rule of law.

propositions.text: RAD cannot be expected to comb evidence and guess why appellants believe RPD erred.
propositions.quote: The RAD cannot be expected to comb the documentary evidence and guess why the Appellants believe the RPD erred.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellants' submissions vague or absent; Federal Court requires explanation of document impact; RAD cannot guess RPD errors without guidance.

propositions.text: RAD will not admit these documents as new evidence and must proceed without oral hearing regarding them.
propositions.quote: The RAD will not admit these documents as new evidence in this appeal. As such, in respect to these documents, the RAD must proceed without an oral hearing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD refuses to admit these documents as new evidence and will proceed without an oral hearing on them.

propositions.text: The determinative issue is the availability of an IFA in Kathmandu in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the determinative issue is the availability of an IFA in Kathmandu in Nepal.

propositions.text: The RPD did not take into account the evidence on the record.
propositions.quote: The Appellants argue: 1. The RPD did not take into account the evidence on the record.

propositions.text: The RPD ignored the Appellants' explanations and the contradictory evidence.
propositions.quote: 2. The RPD ignored the Appellants' explanations and the contradictory evidence.

propositions.text: The RPD finding about how Maoists would locate them in Kathmandu is flawed.
propositions.quote: 3. The RPD finding in respect to the Appellants' testimony about how the Maoists would locate them in Kathmandu is flawed.

propositions.text: There is significant evidence that Maoists have an extensive network throughout Nepal.
propositions.quote: 4. There is significant evidence that the Maoists have an extensive network throughout Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found the key issue is IFA availability in Kathmandu; the Appellants argue the RPD ignored evidence, explanations, and Maoist network evidence.

propositions.text: RAD must apply Rasaratnam two-pronged test for IFA assessment.
propositions.quote: In assessing an IFA, the RAD must apply a two-pronged test cited in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:22

propositions.text: Prong 1: No serious possibility of persecution or risk of cruel treatment in the IFA on balance of probabilities.
propositions.quote: 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA;

propositions.text: Prong 2: Conditions in the IFA must make it reasonable for claimant to seek refuge there.
propositions.quote: 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for the claimant to seek refuge there.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD must apply the Rasaratnam two-pronged test: no serious persecution risk and reasonable conditions to seek refuge in the IFA.

propositions.text: Both prongs must be satisfied to find an IFA.
propositions.quote: Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the Appellants have an IFA.

propositions.text: Once IFA issue raised and potential IFAs identified, burden is on Appellants to show no IFA.
propositions.quote: Once the issue of IFA has been raised and the potential IFAs have been identified, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA.

propositions.text: IFA finding must be based on distinct evaluation of region considering Appellants' identity.
propositions.quote: The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellants' identity.

propositions.text: IFA must be realistic and attainable; no great danger or undue hardship in traveling or staying there.
propositions.quote: An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. The Appellants cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.23

paragraphs.summary: Both Rasaratnam prongs must be met; burden on Appellants to disprove IFA; IFA must be realistic and safe for them.

propositions.text: Canadian courts hold large urban areas cannot be assumed IFA by population size alone.
propositions.quote: Canadian courts have held that large urban areas cannot be assumed to be an IFA by virtue of their population size alone,24

propositions.text: Distance from persecutors does not alone establish IFA viability.
propositions.quote: the distance between the proposed IFA and the location of the persecutors does not in itself serve to establish that the proposed IFA is viable.25

propositions.text: IFA need not be far from origin if it is truly a refuge from persecution in home district.
propositions.quote: the concept of an IFA does not require that the safe haven be in another city or province than the place of origin so long as it is truly an area in which the appellant can seek refuge from the persecution experienced in her home district.26

propositions.text: Whether Appellants face serious possibility of persecution in proposed IFA depends on evidence and these principles.
propositions.quote: Ultimately, the question of whether an appellant has shown, on a balance of probabilities, that they face a serious possibility of persecution in the proposed IFA will turn on their evidence, keeping in mind the general principles above.

paragraphs.summary: Canadian courts say urban size and distance don't alone determine IFA; evidence decides if serious persecution risk exists there.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence describes Maoists as fragmented groups, some part of government, others opposed and violent.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence describes the Maoists in Nepal as a series of groups with various fragments or splinter offshoots. The documentary evidence states, "some of these groups are part of the government, while others are opposed to the government and are engaged in boycotts and violent activities [citation omitted]."27

propositions.text: Some Maoist factions reject government accommodation and engage in extortion.
propositions.quote: There are a number of Maoist factions who have rejected accommodation with the elected government and continue political activity beyond the mainstream Maoist party," elements of which may be involved in extortion [citation omitted]."28

paragraphs.summary: Documentary evidence shows Maoists are fragmented; some part of government, others oppose it and engage in extortion.

propositions.text: Kidnapping and extortion by Maoists are increasingly rare politically; no organized human rights abuses by Maoist party.
propositions.quote: instances of kidnapping and extortion by Maoist groups "are increasingly rare occurrences from a political party perspective" and are "not common any longer."... organized human rights violations/abuses are not taking place in Nepal due to the Maoist party,"

propositions.text: Some criminal activity by former combatants in parts of Nepal may occur.
propositions.quote: although there may be involvement in some criminal activities by "former, frustrated combatants in certain parts of Nepal."29

paragraphs.summary: Kidnapping and extortion by Maoists are rare politically; some criminal acts by former combatants may occur.

propositions.text: Many splinter Maoist groups have broken from central Maoist identity and values.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that many of these splinter groups have broken away from the central "Maoist" identity and values.

propositions.text: Appellants' problems were with local Biplav faction, a Maoist splinter group.
propositions.quote: all of the Appellants' problems with the Maoists occurred in their home area with a separatist Maoist faction (a splinter group) described as the Biplav faction (Netra Bikram Chand Biplav).30

paragraphs.summary: Many Maoist splinter groups broke from central identity; Appellants' issues were with local Biplav faction.

propositions.text: Biplav faction is dissident, outside government, involved in extortion mainly outside Kathmandu in Mid-West and Far-West Nepal.
propositions.quote: this group, composed of former, frustrated combatants and other factions that have rejected accommodation with the elected government,31 is involved in criminal activity and extortion... mainly outside of Kathmandu in the Mid-West and Far-West regions of Nepal.32

propositions.text: Biplav group has disrupted elections in Kathmandu; authorities aggressively curtail their presence there.
propositions.quote: there is evidence that the Biplav group has participated in activities designed to disrupt elections in Kathmandu... authorities have taken an aggressive stance in curtailing the groups' presence in Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: Biplav faction is dissident, extorts mainly outside Kathmandu; disrupted elections in Kathmandu; authorities curtail their presence.

propositions.text: Evidence does not show Biplav Maoists active in extortion/kidnapping of similar profile individuals in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: the evidence does not indicate that they have been active in extortion and kidnapping of individuals with a profile similar to the Appellants in Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: No evidence Biplav Maoists extort or kidnap similar individuals in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Appellants' problems and extortion demands were local to home area, 280 km from Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: the Appellants' problems, as described in their testimony, and the supporting documents submitted, all centred in their home area in XXXX, some 280 km from Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Appellants stayed in Kathmandu for three months without problems before leaving for Canada.
propositions.quote: The Appellants left the area in April 2017 and stayed in Kathmandu for three months without any problems from the agent of persecution before they left for Canada.

propositions.text: Living safely for three months in Kathmandu does not prove it is safe or reasonable.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that living safely for three months in Kathmandu does not confirm that the location is reasonable or safe.

propositions.text: If Maoists were persistent and able, they would have found Appellants in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it reasonable to believe that if this group was persistent in its extortion and pursuit of the Appellants, and if they had the ability, they would have discovered the Appellants in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Appellants' children remain with grandparents in Kathmandu without problems.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes that the Appellants two children have remained with their grandparents in Kathmandu without any reported problems.

paragraphs.summary: Appellants' problems were local; they stayed safely in Kathmandu three months; Maoists likely would have found them if able.

propositions.text: RPD found limited evidence Maoists have nationwide network or strong interregional connections.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the objective evidence provides limited support for the Appellants' assertion that the Maoists have a nationwide network and operate throughout the country; and, found little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the larger Maoist network.

propositions.text: Appellants submit evidence confirms Maoists have nationwide network able to find them anywhere in Nepal.
propositions.quote: The Appellants submit that the evidence confirms the Maoists have a nationwide network, giving them the ability to find them anywhere in Nepal.

propositions.text: Appellants say RPD and documentary evidence confirm Maoist nationwide network.
propositions.quote: The Appellants further submit that the RPD as well as the documentary evidence confirm this fact.

propositions.text: RAD is not persuaded by Appellants' argument about Maoist nationwide network.
propositions.quote: The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellants.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found limited evidence of Maoist nationwide network; Appellants argue otherwise; RAD rejects their argument.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant's explanation of Maoist communication ability is speculative and provides little support.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the principal Appellant's explanation provides little support for his allegations as to the Maoist's communication ability, and that this explanation amounts to simple speculation.

paragraphs.summary: Principal Appellant's explanation of Maoist communication ability is speculative and unsupported.

propositions.text: IRB evidence states YCL has nationwide network but no details on communication or coordination with Biplav Maoists.
propositions.quote: the IRB's objective evidence makes a statement that the Young Communist League (YCL), a youth offshoot of the Maoist party, has a "nationwide network,"33 but beyond that, the detailed information in this document addressing the actions of the YCL towards those associated with opposing political views provides no additional information about the ability of various divisions to communicate and share information throughout the country.

propositions.text: No evidence of linkage or communication between YCL and Biplav Maoists.
propositions.quote: The RAD further notes the documentary evidence does not confirm any linkage between the YCL and the Biplav Maoists.

propositions.text: No evidence Maoist factions communicate or share information due to opposing political views.
propositions.quote: Nor does it make any mention of the ability of the numerous Maoist factions to communicate with each other or whether they would have any interest in sharing information due to their opposing political viewpoints.

propositions.text: Little evidence shows strength of connections or coordination among Maoist groups regarding Appellants' circumstances.
propositions.quote: The RAD's review of the documentary evidence finds little evidence to demonstrate the strength of the connections between regions within the large number of Maoist groups and if/how the different regions coordinate and share information including in circumstances such as the Appellants'.

paragraphs.summary: IRB evidence shows YCL has nationwide network but no link or coordination with Biplav Maoists; little evidence of Maoist group coordination.

propositions.text: Nepal's communication infrastructure was destroyed in 2015 earthquake; telephone poor, mobile fair, internet low penetration.
propositions.quote: Nepal's telephone communication system is described as "poor," its mobile- cellular network is described as "fair," and internet penetration is 17.6 percent of the population.

propositions.text: Communication is limited; Appellants' and documentary statements about Maoist network are vague and unsupported.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the documentary evidence confirms that communication is limited. The RAD finds the singular statement in the documentary evidence, as well as the Appellants' statements about the Maoist "network," are vague and non-specific and they are not supported by any additional evidence before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Nepal's communication infrastructure is poor; Maoist network statements are vague and unsupported.

propositions.text: Insufficient evidence supports Appellants' claim that Biplav Maoists can communicate nationwide to locate them.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds on its review of all of the evidence, that there is insufficient persuasive evidence to support the Appellants' allegations that the local Biplav Maoists in their home area have an ability to communicate throughout Nepal in order to locate the Appellants.

propositions.text: Appellants' problems are limited and local to XXXX; RAD supports RPD findings; Appellants' argument fails.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds the Appellants' problems are limited and local to XXXX. The RAD supports the findings of the RPD in this issue and the Appellants' argument must fail.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds insufficient evidence Biplav Maoists can communicate nationwide; problems are local; supports RPD; Appellants' argument fails.

propositions.text: To target Appellants in Kathmandu, agent must learn they returned, relocated there, and their whereabouts.
propositions.quote: the agent of persecution would be required to: 1) Learn the Appellants have returned to Nepal; 2) Learn the Appellants have relocated to Kathmandu; and, 3) Determine the whereabouts of the Appellants in Kathmandu.

paragraphs.summary: Agent of persecution must learn Appellants returned, relocated to Kathmandu, and their whereabouts to target them there.

propositions.text: If organization had strength to learn return or presence in any city, objective evidence would support this.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds it reasonable to expect that if an organization was of sufficient strength and reach to be able to learn of a person's return to Nepal, or their presence in any city in the country, there would be objective evidence to support this.

paragraphs.summary: If organization could learn of return or presence in any city, objective evidence would exist to support that.

propositions.text: No sufficient credible evidence that Biplav Maoists can trace Appellants' return or movements in Nepal.
propositions.quote: there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellants' return to Nepal upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellants' movements within Nepal.

propositions.text: Appellants were targeted by local Biplav Maoists but no evidence of operational capacity or reach nationwide.
propositions.quote: as much as it accepts that the Appellants were targeted by local individuals whom they identified as members of the Biplav Maoists, there is not sufficient credible evidence to establish that they have the operational capacity or geographic reach to learn of the Appellants' return to Nepal upon arrival at a regular port of entry to the country, or trace the Appellants' movements within Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: No credible evidence Biplav Maoists can trace Appellants' return or movements nationwide despite local targeting.

propositions.text: RPD found it objectively reasonable for Appellants to reside in Kathmandu given their circumstances.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that when it considered the Appellants' particular circumstances, it was objectively reasonable for them to reside in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: Principal Appellant stated no problems if Maoists not targeting them.
propositions.quote: The principal Appellant stated that they would not have any problems if the Maoists were not targeting them.

propositions.text: Appellants did not provide additional testimony or reasons why they could not reside in Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: The Appellants did not advance any additional testimony or provide reasons in their Memorandum as to why they would not be able to reside in the proposed IFA location.

propositions.text: Appellants have 12 years education including 2 years post-secondary.
propositions.quote: The Appellants both have twelve years of education, which includes 2 years of post-secondary schooling.35

propositions.text: Appellants are fluent in Nepali and English.
propositions.quote: Both Appellants are fluent in the Nepali language as well as English.

propositions.text: Appellants have extensive optical business work experience.
propositions.quote: The principal and associate Appellants have extensive work experience in the optical business.36

propositions.text: Appellants have friends and family in Kathmandu likely to assist relocation.
propositions.quote: The Appellants have friends and family members in Kathmandu who would likely be available to assist the Appellants in their relocation.

propositions.text: Appellants previously relocated within Nepal and are experienced international travellers.
propositions.quote: The Appellants provided testimony to indicate that they had relocated in Nepal on a previous occasion. The Appellants are experienced international travellers.

propositions.text: Appellants travelled to Canada and resettled without significant problems.
propositions.quote: They have travelled to Canada and resettled without reporting any significant problems.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found it reasonable for Appellants to reside in Kathmandu; Appellants have education, language, work, family, travel experience.

propositions.text: Given Appellants' circumstances, relocating to Kathmandu is not unduly harsh or unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds after a review of all of the evidence, that given the Appellants' personal circumstances, it is not unduly harsh or objectively unreasonable for the Appellants to relocate to Kathmandu in Nepal.

paragraphs.summary: RAD finds relocating to Kathmandu is not unduly harsh or unreasonable for Appellants given their circumstances.

propositions.text: The RAD agrees with the RPD that Kathmandu offers a viable IFA within Nepal, so the claim fails on this basis.
propositions.quote: the RAD agrees with the conclusion of the RPD for the same reasons - that Kathmandu offers the Appellants a viable IFA within Nepal; the claim therefore fails on this basis.

propositions.text: The RPD concluded Kathmandu is a viable IFA for the Appellants.
propositions.quote: the conclusion of the RPD for the same reasons - that Kathmandu offers the Appellants a viable IFA within Nepal

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees with the RPD that Kathmandu is a viable IFA, so the claim fails on this basis.

propositions.text: Once an IFA is named, the burden is on the Appellants to show the Rasaratnam test's two prongs are not met.
propositions.quote: Once the IFA has been named, the burden is on the Appellants to show that either of the two prongs of the Rasaratnam test are not met.

propositions.text: There is insufficient evidence that Biplav Maoists could locate the Appellants elsewhere in Nepal, including Kathmandu.
propositions.quote: There is insufficient evidence in the record to suggest that the Biplav Maoists from their home region would have the reach or influence to locate the Appellants elsewhere in Nepal, including specifically in Kathmandu.

propositions.text: The Maoists could not enlist other factions to search nationally to create a serious risk of persecution or harm to the Appellants.
propositions.quote: The RAD further finds that they would not be able to enlist other Maoist factions to conduct a national search for the Appellants, such that it would give rise to a serious possibility of persecution or subject them personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture.

propositions.text: The Appellants have not shown the proposed IFA would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh in their circumstances.
propositions.quote: Likewise, they have not demonstrated that in their personal circumstances, the proposed IFA would be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh.

propositions.text: The burden rests with the Appellants to show they do not have an IFA once raised, and they have not discharged it.
propositions.quote: As noted above, the burden of proof rests with the Appellants to show that they do not have an IFA to Kathmandu once raised, and the RAD finds that the Appellants have not discharged that burden.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds insufficient evidence that Maoists could find the Appellants in Kathmandu or that the IFA is unreasonable; burden on Appellants not discharged.

propositions.text: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision that the Appellants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD decision denying refugee protection to the Appellants.
